resolved.explanation: Deleting s13 removed the wrong framing but not the omission. Wilson's unsubsidized NPV is computed against like-for-like replacement of the existing equipment at the end of its life (L705-L716; incremental cost over the reference equipment, L444-L456), so the 59% and 55% are already the buy-at-replacement case. The script never says so, then calls timing 'the other factor' (s31), shows paybacks under a year at failure (s34), asks 'payback compared with what' (s56) and says your group depends on 'whether your old equipment needs replacing anyway' (s59). A viewer will believe buying at replacement lifts the odds above these shares; the model says the shares already are that case. The cited passage does not carry the baseline, so the fix needs evidence first.
resolved.suggestion: Record L705-L716 through record-sources (a verdict on the payback claim) and say in s14 that the comparison is with replacing the old equipment like for like when it wears out.

resolved.explanation: Deetjen also counts only the extra cost of a heat pump over replacing the existing heater with a similar one, assuming the purchase happens when the heater is nearing the end of its life (L499-L506). The 21% is therefore already the replacement-time result, and the same misreading as s14 follows from s31-s36 and s59: a viewer will think replacing at end of life lifts a home above the 21%.
resolved.suggestion: Record L499-L506 through record-sources and say the model already assumes the heat pump is bought when the old heater needs replacing (a clause in s17, or one sentence after it covering both models).

resolved.explanation: The sentence explains the disagreement as one of measure: the national lab model on bills, the second model 'counting the cost of the equipment too'. But the national lab model also counts equipment cost and finds the opposite of Deetjen: the minimum-efficiency heat pump has positive unsubsidized NPV for a group that 'includes most homes that use fuel oil' (L497-L503). A viewer will believe that once equipment cost is counted, leaving oil loses money; the corpus has two lifetime models that disagree on oil. That passage is already in this package, cited by s15 and s21 on the payback claim.
resolved.suggestion: Drop 'counting the cost of the equipment too' and give the national lab model's lifetime result for oil as its own assertion on the payback claim citing L497-L520: counting equipment cost, it found most oil-heated homes came out ahead with a basic unit; the second model found most lose money, in part because most oil homes are in cold climates.

resolved.explanation: The denominators are now named and 55% is correctly the best single heat pump. But the closing figures come right after s56 asks 'payback compared with what, a new furnace and air conditioner, or nothing at all?', and nothing in the script answers it for these two models: both are against like-for-like replacement at end of life. Resolves with the s14 and s17 findings.
resolved.suggestion: Once the baseline passages are recorded, add 'even when bought at replacement time'.

resolved.explanation: The rev 1 blocking problem (gas advice resting on the Minnesota propane table) is fixed and the gas claim is supported by Deetjen and RMI. But 'it paid only when the furnace and air conditioner were being replaced together' is stronger than the passage: the same RMI sentence also lists customers who bundle rooftop solar with electrification, which RMI models for an Oakland gas retrofit (L1194-L1203). The models also price the gas case at replacement rather than with both units working (see s14, s17), so the 'working fine' clause holds a fortiori, not as what they modelled.
resolved.suggestion: '...it paid mainly when the furnace and air conditioner were being replaced together', or drop 'only'.

resolved.explanation: 'In one group of homes' fixes the rev 1 finding. But 'let a smaller, more efficient heat pump do the job' can be heard as insulation letting the homeowner choose a more efficient unit; the passage says the medium- and high-efficiency units already modelled could be smaller ($4,000 and $2,500 lower installed cost), not that insulating enables a more efficient one.
resolved.suggestion: '...let the medium- and high-efficiency heat pumps be smaller, cutting their installed cost by $2,500 to $4,000.'

resolved.explanation: The first clause (switching a working gas system early is worse than anything the models priced) follows a fortiori from their replacement-time baseline and is fine. But 'even at replacement time they found gas homes rarely came out ahead' attributes Deetjen's 'rarely produces a benefit' (the only passage cited, L646-L654) to both models. The national lab model found the opposite for a large group: its positive-NPV group for the minimum-efficiency unit 'also [includes] most homes that use natural gas and have central AC in warmer climates' (L497-L503), the same passage s29 relies on for oil, and s25 has 38-99% of gas homes with AC saving on bills. A gas-heated viewer in a warm climate with central AC, at replacement time, would be told both models say they rarely come out ahead when one says most do.
resolved.suggestion: '...and even at replacement time the second model found gas homes rarely came out ahead, while the national lab model's winners were mostly warm-climate gas homes that already had central air.' At minimum, 'the second model found'.

resolved.explanation: No double counting remains, but the contrast is not right for the national lab model. Its reference scenario replaces heating and cooling equipment at the same time (L429-L433; 'all heating and cooling equipment is replaced', L1269-L1272), so its 55% already is the furnace-and-air-conditioner-together case. Setting 'the case the national figures already describe' against 'replacing a failed furnace and air conditioner together' tells the viewer the about-a-year result lies beyond the national figures, and leaves unexplained why the same timing gives about a year in one Minnesota cost example (a propane-backup system priced from a cost database, propane furnace baseline) but a lifetime gain for at most 55% of homes nationally (s58). Deetjen, by contrast, credits only the heater (L527-L531), so for it the both-together case is indeed better timing.
resolved.suggestion: Scope the about-a-year result to the one Minnesota example and drop the implied contrast, e.g. 'Buying when the old equipment is due is the case the national figures already describe; in the Minnesota example, replacing a failed furnace and air conditioner together turned decades of payback into about a year, a much better result than the national averages for the same timing.'

resolved.explanation: 'Already give the heat pump its best timing' is right for the national lab model, which replaces heating and cooling together (L1269-L1272), but not for Deetjen, which credits only the replacement of the existing heater (equation 3, L500-L506; replacement cost by heater fuel, L527-L531) and not an air conditioner due at the same time. The script's own field evidence (s34, s39) shows replacing both together is better timing than replacing the heater alone. s62's 'the good-timing case' is accurate; 'best' is stronger than one of the two passages.
resolved.suggestion: 'Both of those national figures already assume good timing; the field data show what it costs to switch before the old equipment is due.'
